questions: When I'm anxious, I tend to spend money to relieve tension.
I have bought things I hid from my spouse or family.
I feel momentary pleasure when buying, but regret afterward.
I have expenses I prefer no one knows about.
I use consumption as emotional escape (boredom, loneliness, frustration).
I buy things to appear successful to others.
I own assets (car, clothes, electronics) that cost more than my income warranted.
I have debts that arose from wanting to maintain a lifestyle above my means.
I prioritize appearance and comfort before having an emergency fund.
I feel I need to show material progress to be respected.
I'm afraid to look at my bank statements or debts.
I believe money is 'difficult' or 'not for me'.
My family always struggled financially and I internalized that this is how it should be.
I freeze when I need to make financial decisions.
I cannot think about investments or growth — only survival.

trilha1.diagnostico: Your main pattern is emotional impulse spending. You use purchases as an escape valve for anxiety, boredom, loneliness or frustration. The pleasure is momentary, but regret accumulates. There may be secret spending or "financial infidelity" — consumption you hide from those you love.
trilha1.gatilho: The root trigger is tied to the pursuit of quick dopamine. When emotion is uncomfortable, the brain seeks immediate relief through consumption. Over time, this becomes a cycle: tension → purchase → relief → guilt → more tension.
trilha1.sabedoria: In Jewish tradition, the "yetzer hara" (evil inclination) is not destroyed — it is redirected. The impulse is not the enemy; the impulse without direction is. The Talmud teaches that whoever governs their impulses is stronger than one who conquers cities.
trilha1.proverbio: "Whoever governs their impulses is stronger than one who conquers cities." — Pirkei Avot 4:1
trilha1.metodo: The Jewish method for compulsion is Tikun (repair): pause before action, name the feeling and redirect the energy. Instead of fighting the impulse, you observe it, name it and choose consciously. With each 90-second pause, you strengthen your "muscle of choice".

trilha2.diagnostico: Your main pattern is building "on top" before having the foundation. You invest in appearance, comfort and status before having a reserve, paying off debts and real structure. The house looks beautiful, but the foundation is fragile.
trilha2.gatilho: The root trigger is the need for external validation. The ego seeks recognition through material possessions. Status-driven debts are the symptom; the cause is confusing wealth with appearance.
trilha2.sabedoria: Proverbs 24:27 teaches: "First prepare the field, then build the house." In Jewish tradition, order matters. Before displaying, protect. Before decorating, lay the foundation. The wise person first builds what no one sees — the foundation.
trilha2.proverbio: "First prepare the field, then build the house." — Proverbs 24:27
trilha2.metodo: The Jewish method for financial ego is priority inversion: reserve before luxury, debt payoff before acquisition, simplicity before ostentation. With each decision, ask: "Does this strengthen my foundation or just my facade?"

trilha3.diagnostico: Your main pattern is paralysis through fear. Past financial traumas, inherited scarcity beliefs and fear of loss create a prison where you don't advance. Surviving has become the ceiling; prospering seems impossible or "not for you".
trilha3.gatilho: The root trigger is financial trauma — yours or your family's. Memories of difficulty created an internal narrative that money is dangerous, scarce or "not for people like me". This generates decision paralysis.
trilha3.sabedoria: The Torah repeats "Do not fear" 365 times — one for each day of the year. In Jewish tradition, fear is acknowledged, but it does not have the final word. Deuteronomy 30:19 says: "I have set before you life and death; choose life." You have the power to choose, even with fear.
trilha3.proverbio: "Do not fear, for I am with you." — Isaiah 41:10
trilha3.metodo: The Jewish method for financial fear is gradual action with faith. It does not require total courage — it requires the first step. Investing $10, asking for a raise, looking at your bank statement. Each small action proves to the brain that the danger is not as great as fear suggests.
